We report a first-in-human clinical trial evaluating the safety and immunogenicity of a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) vaccine expressing the SUDV envelope glycoprotein (rVSVΔG-SEBOV-GP). Methods In this single-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation phase 1 trial, adults (18–50 years) in good general health and without previous exposure to VSV-vectored vaccines or any haemorrhagic fever, were enrolled at two clinical research sites in Texas, USA. Participants received a single intramuscular dose of rVSVΔG-SEBOV-GP at 2 × 10 6 , 2 × 10 7 , or 2 × 10 8 plaque-forming units, or placebo. Dose groups were enrolled sequentially, from the lowest to the highest dose. In each dose group, the first two participants (sentinels) received the vaccine without randomisation; the remaining were randomised (4:1 vaccine-to-placebo ratio, for a final vaccine-to-placebo ratio of 5:1). Only participants were masked. Primary outcomes, assessed on all participants, were safety and tolerability assessments, based on local and systemic reactions within 14 days, and vaccine-related serious adverse events and adverse events of special interest for the entire trial. Secondary outcome was the evaluation of humoral immunity, assessed by anti-SUDV-GP IgG and serum neutralising activity against SUDV-GP at baseline and 28, 84, and 168 days after vaccination. This study (now completed) is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05724472). Findings Between June 19, 2023, and July 21, 2023, 36 participants (20 [56%] women; median age 37 years [IQR=12·2]) were enrolled and received a single intramuscular injection of vaccine (n=10 per dose group) or placebo (n=6); all vaccine recipients completed 6 months of follow-up. 31 (86%) of 36 (vaccine 26 [87%] of 30; placebo five [83%] of six) participants had solicited adverse events; the proportions were similar across all dose groups. Most participants (vaccine 22 [73%] of 30; placebo five [83%] of six) had local pain and tenderness, mild to moderate, but severe in one participant (2 × 10 8 plaque-forming units). Systemic reactions occurred in 25 (83%) of 30 vaccine recipients and four (67%) of six placebo recipients. Severe transient reactions were reported by one (17%) of six placebo recipients (joint pain) and four (13%) of 30 vaccine recipients (combinations of malaise, chills, myalgia, abdominal pain, headache, and nausea). Antibody responses, present by day 29 and beyond, were similar at all dosages, and maintained in all participants by month 6. By the end of the study, neutralising activity was detected in 20 (67%) of 30 vaccinees and correlated to binding IgG. Interpretation rVSVΔG-SEBOV-GP was well tolerated and immunogenic at all the three doses studied. These findings support its further development for prevention of SVD. Funding Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority.

title: Antimicrobial resistance surveillance: a crucial pillar for sustainable leprosy control and chemoprophylaxis
abstract: Leprosy, also known as Hansen´s disease, remains a public health concern, with around 200 000 new cases reported worldwide each year. Recent strategies to reduce transmission include post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) with single-dose rifampicin, which has shown moderate protective efficacy and is being increasingly implemented on scale. However, widespread rifampicin use outside combination therapy raises concerns regarding the potential emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Mycobacterium leprae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Although AMR in leprosy is less common than that in tuberculosis, resistance to rifampicin, dapsone, and fluoroquinolones highlights the need for systematic surveillance. However, AMR surveillance remains inconsistently implemented, with inadequate laboratory capacity, insufficient political prioritisation, and fragmented global coordination posing major barriers. In this Personal View, we argue that AMR surveillance should be an integral component of leprosy control and PEP programmes. We outline key challenges and propose pragmatic policy recommendations, including strengthening laboratory capacity, integrating surveillance into national programmes, and leveraging existing tuberculosis diagnostic networks. Embedding AMR surveillance within PEP strategies supports the long-term effectiveness of treatment and prevention efforts while minimising unintended consequences for global health.

title: Transmission of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae in a Malawian neonatal unit: a clinical and genomic analysis of a prospective cohort study
abstract: Background Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important cause of neonatal sepsis in sub-Saharan Africa and is frequently antimicrobial resistant. In this study, we investigated key transmission routes of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae (ESBL- K pneumoniae ) within a single neonatal unit to inform development of contextually appropriate infection prevention and control practices. Methods We recruited a prospective mother and neonate cohort of babies admitted for less than 48 h and expected to stay for 24 h or more, where the mother or guardian was aged 18 years or older. Participants were followed up until day 7 of admission or discharge, with samples taken on day 1 and 3, and at the final follow-up (maternal stool, neonatal stool, maternal hands, cots, and swaddling cloth [day 1 only]). We sampled the ward environment weekly and included contemporaneous invasive ESBL- K pneumoniae isolates in our analysis. The primary outcome was ESBL- K pneumoniae colonisation . K pneumoniae single-colony isolates were subjected to single-colony whole-genome sequencing, and plate-sweeps had post-enrichment metagenomics performed, before evaluation of multilocus sequence types and single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Statistical analyses (Kaplan–Meier, state-transition models, source-attribution models, transmission analysis combining single-nucleotide polymorphisms and timing of sample collection, and exponential random graph models) were used to infer whether transmission occurred and from which sources. Findings We recruited 94 neonate–mother pairs (from July 23, 2019, to March 30, 2020). Median gestational age was 37 (IQR 35–38) weeks, 41 (44%) of the 94 neonates were girls, all were of Black ethnicity, and 69 (73%) of 94 neonates were antibiotic exposed. ESBL- K pneumoniae rapidly colonised neonates (Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated median 5 days [95% CI 4–6]), with 44 (49%) of 90 of neonates being colonised at least once. State-transition model indicated females had increased colonisation risk (hazard ratio 2·33 [95% credible interval 1·07–5·40]). Invasive isolates (13 [76%] of 17) clustered with stool and environmental isolates. Results of transmission analysis using single-colony whole-genome sequencing and post-enrichment metagenomics were consistent with ESBL- K pneumoniae transmission from cots (13–29%), ward surfaces (37–65%; especially sinks and oxygen delivery equipment), mother's hands (6–13%), and other neonates (8–13%). The results of network analysis (exponential random graph models) were consistent with shared cots increasing transmission risk from 5·7 × 10 −5 (95% CI 1·4 × 10 −5 to 2·3 × 10 −4 ) to 5·9 × 10 −4 (3·1 × 10 −4 to 1·1 × 10 −3 ). Interpretation The hospital environment is implicated in colonisation and invasive infection with ESBL- K pneumoniae . Infection prevention and control interventions should focus on containing neonatal stool, maternal hand hygiene, cot decontamination, single-use oxygen delivery equipment, and surface cleaning, particularly sinks. Funding Medical Research Council (UK); National Institute for Health Research (UK); Gates Foundation (USA); Wellcome (UK).

title: Metabolism as a missing link between diabetes, tuberculosis, and drug resistance?
abstract: Diabetes affects approximately one in ten adults globally, and its prevalence is expected to rise substantially over the coming decades. Diabetes doubles the risk of tuberculosis and is also associated with drug-resistant tuberculosis, adding to the global health and socioeconomic impact of tuberculosis. Increased exposure to drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates or selection of resistance mutations owing to non-adherence or low drug levels during treatment are unlikely to fully explain this association. Instead, we hypothesise that metabolism is the missing link. First, diabetes might provide a more permissive immunometabolic environment for M tuberculosis, which could compensate for the metabolic fitness costs of some drug resistance mutations. Second, the higher mutational burden of M tuberculosis reported in individuals with diabetes and tuberculosis might lead to greater antibiotic resistance. Finally, drug tolerance might be favoured in diabetes and act as an intermediate step towards canonical drug resistance mutations. These hypotheses can be tested through comprehensive epidemiological studies, phenotypic testing and sequencing of M tuberculosis isolates from people with and without diabetes, and experimental in vitro or animal studies. A better understanding of these mechanisms could improve prevention and treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis among people with diabetes.

title: Evaluation of blood culture bottles and instruments for cost, affordability, and supply chain to meet global equity in sepsis diagnostics
abstract: We read with great interest the recent Article by Anke Breine and colleagues,1 published in The Lancet Microbe, which evaluated blood culture bottles (BCBs) from newer companies entering the international market (Autobio, DL-Biotech, and Mindray) and compared these with established BCBs such as bioMérieux. An extensive panel of pathogens was assessed using a spiked sample method. Autobio, DL-Biotech, and Mindray paediatric BCBs were compared with the bioMérieux BacT/ALERT 3D, and the results suggest the competitive utility of the lesser-known BCB brands.

title: AMR stewardship needs microbiology
abstract: 30 years ago, McGowan and Gerding published a review titled: “Does antibiotic restriction prevent resistance?” Their 1996 review is often cited as being the first to apply “stewardship” to the preservation of antimicrobial effectiveness, a term that has firmly entered the lexicon of preventing the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Since its publication, many studies have investigated the effect of stewardship interventions. Such studies are usually well designed with altruistic aims and encouraging results that have informed policy.

title: Highlights of ICOPA 2026
Data-driven diagnostic reform in Ethiopia's transition to pLDH-based malaria rapid diagnostic tests amid rising pfhrp2/3 deletions: a multisite, facility-based, cross-sectional study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rising histidine-rich protein (HRP) 2 and 3 gene deletions undermine the reliability of HRP2-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) that are widely used to detect Plasmodium falciparum. In such settings, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)-based RDTs, targeting an alternative antigen, might provide a useful diagnostic option. We aimed to assess the performance of HRP2-based and LDH-based RDTs among febrile patients across six districts in Ethiopia representing diverse transmission intensities, varying pfhrp2/3 deletion frequencies, and differing levels of Plasmodium vivax co-endemicity. METHODS: This multisite, facility-based, cross-sectional study was based in health centres from six districts in Ethiopia: Abobo, Arba Minch Zuria, Fentale, Gondar Zuria, Metema, and Pawe. The study recruited patients aged at least 6 months who had a fever (axillary temperature ≥37·5°C) or a history of fever within the preceding 24 h. The diagnostic performance of SD Bioline HRP2/PvLDH (Bioline), BIOCREDIT PfLDH/PvLDH (BIOCREDIT Pf/Pv), and BIOCREDIT HRP2/PfLDH (BIOCREDIT Pf-dual) RDTs was assessed against microscopy and qPCR targeting 18S rRNA. Plasmodium antigens were quantified using multiplex Luminex, whereas pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 exon 2 deletions were detected using digital PCR. The primary outcome was diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of each RDT compared with microscopy and qPCR. RDT performance was analysed by species, parasite density, site, and pfhrp2/3 gene deletion status, ensuring evaluation across diverse transmission settings. FINDINGS: 1800 participants (median age 20 [IQR 12-30]; 56·4% male) were enrolled between Sept 2, 2021, and Feb 5, 2022. One dried blood spot sample was lost; qPCR confirmed infection in 1055 (58·6%) of 1799 participants, comprising 739 (70·1%) P falciparum, 166 (15·7%) P vivax, and 150 (14·2%) mixed infections. Pfhrp2/3 deletions varied, with double deletions reaching 52 (35·1%) of 148 infections in Gondar Zuria. Using microscopy as a reference, the solely HRP2-based Bioline RDT showed reduced P falciparum sensitivity (75·7% [95% CI 73·7-77·6]), particularly in deletion-affected areas. Excluding deletion cases significantly improved the sensitivity of HRP2-based Bioline RDT (p<0·001), giving 96·7% for wild type versus 7·8% in double deletions. The BIOCREDIT Pf-dual RDT showed a P falciparum sensitivity of 97·1% (95% CI 96·3-97·9), and BIOCREDIT Pf/Pv RDT showed a P falciparum sensitivity of 91·2% (95% CI 90·0-92·5) across all settings. For P vivax, the BIOCREDIT Pf/Pv showed improved sensitivity of 95·7% (95% CI 94·8-96·7), outperforming the Bioline test, which reached 89·9% (95% CI 88·5-91·3). The BIOCREDIT Pf-dual had the lowest detection threshold (90% probability) for P falciparum at 97 parasites per μL, outperforming BIOCREDIT Pf/Pv (133 parasites per μL) and Bioline (2218 parasites per μL). INTERPRETATION: Our findings highlight the high and regionally variable prevalence of pfhrp2/3 gene deletions, which compromise HRP2-based test performance. By integrating diagnostic, genetic, and antigen data, our findings revealed key diagnostic gaps and informed Ethiopia's national policy shift from HRP2-based RDTs to non-HRP2-based (LDH-based) RDTs and offer a model for other countries facing similar diagnostic challenges owing to pfhrp2/3 deletions. FUNDING: The Gates Foundation and Wellcome Trust.

title: Epidemiology and phylogenomic characterisation of the 2025 Ebola virus disease outbreak in Bulape, Kasaï province, Democratic Republic of the Congo: a retrospective observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: An Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in Bulape health zone, Kasaï province, DR Congo, was declared on Sept 4, 2025, and ended on Dec 1, 2025. We describe the dynamics of this outbreak and the molecular characteristics of the causative Ebola virus variant (species Orthoebolavirus zairense). METHODS: This retrospective observational study included probable and PCR-confirmed EVD cases reported between Aug 4 and Dec 1, 2025. Individuals who tested PCR-negative for Ebola virus were classified as discarded cases and excluded. Trained field investigators and health professionals recorded epidemiological and clinical data during initial case investigation. The primary outcome was the generation of complete Ebola virus genomes from clinical samples tested PCR-positive. Ebola virus RNA was detected by real-time PCR and subjected to whole-genome sequencing to generate complete Ebola virus genomes. Ebola virus sequences were integrated with detailed epidemiological data to infer case linkages and reconstruct transmission chains. Bayesian analysis was performed to infer time-scaled phylogenetic trees. FINDINGS: In total, 64 EVD cases (53 confirmed and 11 probable) were reported, including 45 deaths, corresponding to a case-fatality rate of 70·3% (45 of 64, 95% CI 57·6-81·1%). The median age of affected individuals was 25 years (IQR 6-51) and 58% (37 of 64) were women. Our analysis identified five generations of transmission originating from an undetected index case, with transmission occurring predominantly in health-care settings. One inferred superspreading patient generated 11 secondary infections, indicating marked heterogeneity in early transmission. The mean serial interval was 15·7 days (95% CI 13·9-17·6 days). Two hypothetical unsampled cases were inferred within the transmission chain: one representing the superspreading patient within the chain, and another representing a case that did not lead to any further secondary human-to-human transmission. Phylogenetic analysis showed two distinct clusters, each likely arising from a single source and both sharing a recent common ancestor. The 2025 Ebola virus lineages are most closely related to genome sequences from the 1976 Yambuku-Mayinga outbreak. INTERPRETATION: The 2025 EVD outbreak likely resulted from a novel zoonotic spillover; health care-associated transmission substantially amplified the outbreak. Delayed recognition and inadequate infection prevention and control capacity likely facilitated superspreading. Integrated genomic and epidemiological investigation strengthens transmission chain inference and supports a rapid public health response. Strengthening infection prevention and control measures in health-care facilities, alongside integrated epidemiological-genomic and ecological surveillance, rapid response, and vaccination among health-care workers, is essential to minimising the effect of future EVD outbreaks. FUNDING: WHO; Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention; Culmen International LLC; and the Belgian Directorate-General for Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid under the extended Framework Agreement 5.

title: Evaluation of the laboratory assessment process for A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network (ACORN-LAP) in low-income and middle-income countries: a multicountry, cross-sectional analysis with longitudinal quality monitoring
abstract: BACKGROUND: High-quality microbiology laboratory data underpin effective antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. Laboratory assessments are useful for ensuring the quality of microbiology data used for AMR surveillance, especially in low-income and middle-income countries where accreditation might not be feasible. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the microbiology laboratory assessment and quality monitoring tools developed to assess laboratories participating in A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network 2 (ACORN2). METHODS: We conducted a multicountry observational study of microbiology laboratories participating in the ACORN2 surveillance project, including a baseline cross-sectional laboratory assessment process (ACORN-LAP) with longitudinal quality monitoring and follow-up. Between Sept 21, 2021, to Nov 25, 2024, all laboratories of hospitals identified as ACORN2 sites identified through investigator networks were invited to complete the ACORN-LAP. These laboratories were from nine countries across Asia and Africa. The assessment included an online REDCap-based assessment, and document-based and video call-based reviews by two selected ACORN assessors. The laboratories participated in quarterly quality monitoring processes, including the review of internal quality control (IQC) and external quality assessment (EQA) results. Anonymous feedback was collected, and an in-person feedback session was conducted during the study. The primary evaluation outcome was the findings of the ACORN-LAP, including the number of key and non-key recommendations identified. Secondary evaluation outcomes included quality monitoring performance, laboratory feedback on the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes, and comparison of the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes with existing laboratory assessment tools. FINDINGS: 20 laboratories completed the ACORN-LAP. The median time from initial contact with the laboratory to issuing recommendations was 3 months (IQR 3-4; range 1-8). The assessors identified 144 recommendations (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 3-8·5]; range 2-21), including 46 key and 98 non-key recommendations. Non-accredited laboratories received more recommendations per laboratory than accredited laboratories (median difference 5 [95% CI 1-11]; p=0·0062 and incidence rate ratio (IRR) 2·5 [95% CI 1·56-4·09]; p=0·0002). Non-accredited laboratories also received more key recommendations per laboratory (median difference 2 [95% CI 1-5]; p=0·0030) and IRR 4·75 [95% CI 2·11-11·84]; p=0·0003). 116 quality monitoring forms were completed (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 4-7]; range 2-9). 115 IQC and 59 scored EQA events were reported. Review of such quality monitoring data identified previously undetected IQC failures and led to improved IQC recording in some laboratories. Feedback showed that laboratories considered the assessment process useful although some laboratories found the assessment process labour intensive. INTERPRETATION: The findings support the use of structured laboratory assessment with ongoing quality monitoring to strengthen AMR surveillance, particularly in non-accredited laboratories. A simple, harmonised global online tool with integrated quality monitoring that assesses against a minimum standard could improve the quality and comparability of AMR surveillance data in low-income and middle-income countries. FUNDING: Wellcome Trust.

title: A competitive BB-ELISA for anti-toxin B neutralising antibodies in assessing risk of recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection: a retrospective cohort study from the MODIFY I and II trials
abstract: BACKGROUND: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI) is a major clinical challenge. Host neutralising antibodies (NAbs) against toxin B (TcdB) are key correlates of protection, but the absence of a simple, standardised assay to measure this functional immunity prevents risk-adapted patient management. We aimed to develop and clinically validate a rapid, bispecific antibody-based competitive ELISA for measuring anti-TcdB NAbs. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study of the MODIFY I and II phase 3, randomised, placebo-controlled trials of bezlotoxumab (conducted at 322 sites in 30 countries between Oct 10, 2011, and May 22, 2015), we assessed post-treatment serum samples from placebo-arm participants with CDI after initial clinical cure. We engineered a bispecific antibody (BB-IgG) targeting two conserved neutralising TcdB epitopes and developed a rapid competitive ELISA (BB-ELISA). The assay was standardised into a commercial-grade kit and validated through correlation with a cell-based neutralisation assay. We measured patients' anti-TcdB NAb levels after antibiotic therapy by using BB-ELISA and evaluated their association with the primary outcome (rCDI) within 12 weeks. The prognostic cutoff was determined using classification and regression tree analysis. FINDINGS: =0·7245, p<0·0001). Serum samples from 232 (30%) of 773 eligible placebo-arm patients were analysed using the standardised BB-ELISA. A BB-ELISA threshold of <24% inhibition defined the Low NAb group. The Low NAb group had a significantly higher rCDI rate (57 [33%] of 174) than did patients showing protective response (8 [14%] of 58; p=0·0053). In multivariable analysis, a low NAb response independently predicted rCDI (adjusted odds ratio 3·88, 95% CI 1·58-9·51; p=0·003). INTERPRETATION: The BB-ELISA represents a simple, standardised, and scalable tool for quantifying functional anti-TcdB immunity at the point of cure, filling a long-standing diagnostic gap. This assay identifies patients with CDI who are at high risk of recurrence, thus supporting rapid risk stratification. The assay could help guide personalised management decisions and future targeted therapeutic strategies for rCDI. FUNDING: National Institutes of Health and Merck.

title: MERS-CoV in Africa: a One Health review of the silent reservoir
abstract: Africa harbours more than 80% of the world's dromedary camels, with a pooled MERS-CoV seroprevalence of 73·7%; however, no autochthonous outbreak in humans has been documented. In this Review, we weigh five interacting explanations for the absence of documented human outbreaks based on the strength of the evidence for each explanation. The primary explanation is virological; many, although not all, African clade C MERS-CoV strains show reduced replication competence in human respiratory tissues, and clade C strains have not become established in Arabian camels or humans despite decades of large-scale export from the Horn of Africa into the world's most intensively monitored MERS-CoV surveillance system. Environmental contexts, including dry-season herd aggregation, drought, and calving-linked shedding, influence when MERS-CoV exposure occurs in humans. Surveillance limitations, dispersed exposure among the African population particularly pastoralists, lower comorbidity burden than that in affected populations in the Arabian regions, and absent nosocomial amplification are secondary explanations, largely downstream of the primary factors. Although longitudinal cohort studies using enhanced diagnostics detected sporadic spillover in Africa, these infections were asymptomatic. The presence of clade B strains and interclade B×C recombinants in Egyptian camels are surveillance priorities and not evidence of MERS-CoV emergence in humans. Africa's silent reservoir is therefore not a safe one: continued clade C circulation, alongside emerging clade B introductions and interclade recombinants, could shift this balance, underscoring the need for sustained genomic and human surveillance of the reservoir.

title: Host and environmental factors associated with upper respiratory tract mycobiota in healthy individuals: a cross-sectional observational study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although the bacterial microbiome in the respiratory tract is well-characterised, the fungal microbiome or mycobiome remains underexplored. We aimed to characterise the upper respiratory tract mycobiome within the general population, assess its variation across niches and in relation to host and environmental factors, and evaluate its role as a source community for the fungal pathogens Candida auris (also called Candidozyma auris), Candida albicans, and Aspergillus fumigatus. METHODS: In this cross-sectional population-based observational study, we characterised paired nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal mycobiota from 108 participants in the Dutch population-based PIENTER-3 cohort using internal transcribed spacer-amplicon sequencing. Participants were recruited via municipal registers from four municipalities in the central Netherlands between Feb 1, 2016, and Oct 16, 2017. No clinical inclusion or exclusion criteria were applied. In addition, pan-Aspergillus and A fumigatus qPCR assays were performed on oropharynx samples. The primary outcome was to characterise niche-specific differences in the mycobiota. FINDINGS: We analysed samples from 108 participants (55 [51%] female and 53 [49%] male); the participant age ranged between 10 and 87 years (median 58; IQR 30-67). After quality-control filtering, 107 nasopharyngeal and 89 oropharyngeal samples were retained for analysis. Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal mycobiota differed in composition (p=0·0010) and diversity (p<0·0001), with greater heterogeneity in the oropharynx and higher diversity in the nasopharynx. We identified niche-specific factors influencing community structure; sampling season, degree of urbanisation, and livestock farm exposure shaped the nasopharyngeal mycobiota, particularly influencing the abundance of ubiquitous and plant-associated genera. In contrast, age, degree of urbanisation, and recent antibiotic use were key factors influencing the oropharyngeal mycobiome composition. Candida was highly prevalent in both niches, with the genus being more prevalent in the oropharynx (prevalence=85 [96%] of 89 samples) than in the nasopharynx (58 [54%] of 107 samples). Aspergillus was detected at low relative abundance in both niches and was more prevalent in the nasopharynx (49 [46%] of 107 samples) than in the oropharynx (27 [30%] of 89 samples). Although C albicans was frequently found, with its prevalence increasing with age, A fumigatus was not identified during internal transcribed spacer-amplicon sequencing or qPCR. INTERPRETATION: Our study identified niche-specific fungal communities, with their distinct influencing factors. Our findings also suggest that respiratory mycobiota might serve as a source community for potentially pathogenic fungi. Future studies should investigate which fungi represent commensals versus potential pathogens and elucidate the mechanisms underlying colonisation resistance and infection risk. FUNDING: National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM), Netherlands Organization for Scientific Research, and Chief Scientist Office grant.

title: Importance of faecal sample collection in prospective cohort studies to evaluate the effect of the gut microbiome on cancer development
abstract: The gut microbiome has been linked to cancer in many cross-sectional studies. These studies compared individuals with and without cancer, but they do not establish causation. Prospective cohort studies, with faecal samples collected before a cancer diagnosis, will be instrumental in assessing the role of the gut microbiome in human cancer risk. We identified 18 prospective cohort studies, each of which collected faecal samples from at least 5000 individuals with expected future cancer linkages, and calculated the projected numbers of colorectal, stomach, pancreatic, and female breast cancers. Larger numbers of incident cancer cases need to be evaluated to identify robust associations between the gut microbiome and cancer with sufficient power. To achieve this goal, we propose that additional cohorts collect faecal samples, particularly those with participants from various backgrounds and from under-represented world regions. Furthermore, sufficient data sharing and improved methods are needed to pool and meta-analyse microbiome data. These data can then be used to gain a better understanding of how the gut microbiome is involved in cancer development and other health outcomes at multiple body sites.

title: MERS-CoV: time to reassess the case-fatality rate
abstract: MERS-CoV remains an important zoonotic threat. Since its emergence in 2012, 2649 laboratory-confirmed cases and 960 deaths have been reported globally as of Aug 31, 2026, yielding a crude case-fatality ratio (CFR) of approximately 36%.1 The estimated CFR has become one of the defining epidemiological characteristics of MERS-CoV. Yet, more than 14 years after the virus was identified, is it still appropriate to rely on a single cumulative CFR without greater contextualisation?

title: Transmission potential of Andes virus
abstract: We read with interest the Comment published in The Lancet Microbe by Jason R Andrews and Isaac I Bogoch,1 who highlighted that the largest Andes virus outbreaks are driven by rare superspreading events, whereas most outbreaks undergo rapid stochastic extinction. This finding implies that widespread transmission is unlikely. We agree and note that the basic reproduction number, R0, might be lower than they estimated, further strengthening this conclusion.

title: H5N1 in Australia: psychology, penguins, and preparedness
abstract: The Australian Antarctic Division (AAD) has announced it will withdraw all its staff from the remote Macquarie Island in Antarctica in October, 2026, citing the likelihood of psychosocial stress on its staff in the event of witnessing mass animal deaths from an impending outbreak of H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b lineage).

title: US Executive Order on child vaccines deemed unscientific
abstract: In a move described as “unscientific and dangerous” by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), US President Donald Trump signed an Executive Order on Aug 10, 2026, recommending that children only get vaccinated against 11 diseases, instead of the existing 18 recommended by the AAP. The Order was issued despite “no new evidence to justify significant changes to childhood immunization guidance”, according to a press statement by AAP President Andrew D Racine.

title: Regional expansion and adaptive evolution of multidrug-resistant Candida tropicalis in China: a retrospective, multicentre, genomic study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The emergence of antifungal-resistant Candida tropicalis poses a severe threat to human health and complicates clinical management, yet the molecular epidemiology and mechanisms underlying its resistance and persistence in hospital settings remain poorly understood. We aimed to investigate the regional epidemiology, persistence and virulence trade-offs, and adaptive traits associated with the expansion of multidrug-resistant C tropicalis. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, multicentre, genomic study of C tropicalis isolates from 84 hospitals in east China and included additional multidrug-resistant (resistant to azoles and echinocandins) isolates from active surveillance at Shanghai East Hospital. We analysed clinical metadata from this hospital to identify risk factors for multidrug-resistant isolate recovery and 30-day mortality. We conducted whole-genome sequencing, RNA sequencing, phenotypic assays, and experimental evolution to elucidate resistance mechanisms, virulence dynamics, and adaptive traits. FINDINGS: 1184 clinical isolates from Jan 1, 2017, to Dec 31, 2024, were included; of these, 356 (30·1%) were azole resistant and 98 (8·3%) were multidrug resistant. We identified the regional expansion of a multidrug-resistant C tropicalis lineage, DST849, which accounted for 92 (94%) of 98 multidrug-resistant cases and was predominantly isolated from the urinary tract. Admission to a surgical ward (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 46·37, 95% CI 17·48-123·00) and intubation (32·30, 10·28-101·45) were key risk factors for multidrug-resistant isolate recovery. Multivariable logistic regression revealed that multidrug-resistant C tropicalis isolation was an independent predictor of 30-day mortality (aOR 2·84, 95% CI 1·31-6·16; p=0·0081). Phylogenomic analysis revealed that multidrug-resistant isolates evolved from azole-resistant ancestors (DST225) via the acquisition of FKS1 mutations (S30P) while retaining ERG11 mutations (Y132F and S154F) and acquired a distinguishing ICL1 (Y43T) loss-of-heterozygosity mutation. INTERPRETATION: Our findings reveal the emergence of multidrug-resistant Ctropicalis through lineage-specific expansion, driven by genetic plasticity and adaptive stress responses. These adaptations might facilitate persistence under antifungal and environmental pressures in health-care settings. These insights underscore the urgent need for improved antifungal stewardship, targeted genomic surveillance, and interventions to mitigate multidrug-resistant fungal threats. FUNDING: National Natural Science Foundation of China, Chinese Ministry of Science and Technology.

title: Role of the urobiome in urinary tract infections: current knowledge and research prospects
authors: Justin J J van der Hooft
Janneke H H M van de Wijgert
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly cystitis, are among the most common bacterial infections worldwide, with a disproportionate burden on adult female individuals, who often have recurrence. The discovery of the urobiome, a low microbial biomass community in the urinary tract, has transformed our understanding of UTI pathogenesis and infection susceptibility. Experimental and omics approaches provide insights into the taxonomic and functional complexity of the urobiome, highlighting the importance of microbial metabolites, ecological interactions, and host-microbe dynamics. Polymicrobial interactions within the urobiome further modulate pathogenicity, with some microbes inhibiting or promoting uropathobionts. Advancing UTI management will require combining omics and experimental research with ecological and evolutionary insights. This approach can enable the development of personalised, non-antibiotic interventions, such as live biotherapeutics and prebiotics, to improve diagnostics, reduce antibiotic resistance, and enhance treatment efficacy.

title: The future of cholera genomics through the lens of clinical, public health, and research practitioners in Africa
abstract: Cholera remains a persistent public health threat, complicating efforts to track transmission across borders and undermining control measures. Surveillance systems often remain fragmented and reactive, and many aspects of Vibrio cholerae evolution continue to be challenging, restricting the development of effective, data-driven interventions. Although genomics is increasingly transforming our understanding of cholera by revealing new insights into pathogen biology, transmission dynamics, and evolution, its routine integration into public health practice remains low. In this Personal View, we present the perspectives of those working at the frontline of cholera control in Africa (clinicians, public health practitioners, and researchers) who are rarely heard from, yet who actively shape strategies, navigate technological hurdles, and address system-level challenges to incorporate genomics into routine practice. These insights emerged through the Vibriowatch and Cholera Genomics Course, funded by the Gates Foundation and hosted by the Centre for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia in Lusaka, Zambia, on Feb 9-14, 2025. The course convened 36 participants from 18 African countries to exchange practical experience on how genomic data can be translated into public health decision making. A key outcome of this convening was the establishment of the Community of Practice for Cholera Genomics, which has since evolved into a sustained and structured platform for collaboration, peer learning, and collective problem solving, bringing together practitioners working across cholera surveillance, genomics, and response systems, ensuring that genomic approaches are grounded in local realities and appropriately embedded within cholera-control approaches. The thematic workstreams of the Community of Practice for Cholera Genomics meet regularly to deliver defined technical priorities, with seminar sessions bringing the whole community together to review progress, align priorities, and engage external experts. Accountability is embedded through shared ownership of workplans within each thematic team, with members jointly responsible for tracking progress. Grounded in real-world experience, in this Personal View, we offer timely, policy-relevant recommendations to strengthen genomic approaches, centring African leadership, equity, and long-term sustainability.

title: From reactive to proactive: rethinking parasite controls in the fresh produce chain
abstract: The recent cyclosporiasis outbreak in the USA linked to shredded iceberg lettuce and 2026 WHO estimates of the global, regional, and national burden of 14 foodborne diarrhoeal enteric hazards (2000–21) have once again thrust Cyclospora cayetanensis into the public health spotlight.1,2 Yet focusing solely on Cyclospora risks obscuring a far broader threat, as this outbreak is only the latest reminder that fresh produce such as leafy greens and ready-to-eat (RTE) salads can serve as vectors for a wide spectrum of foodborne parasites, ranging from protozoa such as Cryptosporidium, Giardia, and Toxoplasma gondii to trematode species such as Fasciolopsis buski.

title: Immunogenicity and shedding of live-attenuated intranasal respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in children aged 6–18 months by baseline serostatus: a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 1/2 trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes acute respiratory illness in young children. The live-attenuated RSV vaccine candidate RSV/ΔNS2/Δ1313/I1314L (RSVt) has shown promising immunogenicity and safety in children aged 6-18 months. However, how baseline RSV serostatus influences immunogenicity and viral shedding after RSVt vaccination in young children remains largely unreported. In this phase 1/2 trial, we aimed to evaluate immunogenicity and virus shedding after RSVt vaccination in children aged 6-18 months stratified by baseline RSV serostatus. METHODS: In this multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 1/2 trial, children in the USA (N=22 sites), Chile (N=2 sites), and Honduras (N=2 sites) were recruited as participants. Healthy children aged 6-18 months at enrolment who were born at or after 34 weeks of gestation (if age 1 year or older) or children younger than 1 year at enrolment who were born at or after 37 weeks of gestation were eligible for inclusion. Key exclusion criteria included previous administration of any RSV vaccine or anti-RSV products; administration of an influenza vaccine in the 7 days before enrolment; administration of inactivated vaccines or live-attenuated rotavirus vaccine in the 14 days before enrolment; or administration of any other live vaccines or investigational products in the 28 days before enrolment. Participants were assigned to four sequential cohorts to receive intranasal low-dose RSVt (RSVt-LD) or high-dose RSVt (RSVt-HD), administered once on day 0 or twice on day 0 and day 56, or placebo. Cohort 4 was the primary comparison cohort, and participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) via a centralised interactive response system to receive two administrations of the treatment. Participants, investigators, and outcome assessors were masked to group allocation; only designated staff preparing and administering study interventions were unmasked. The primary outcomes reported were immunogenicity evaluated using serum RSV-neutralisation assays and anti-F IgG ELISA on days 0, 56, and 84 and vaccine virus shedding measured using quantitative RT-PCR on days 7 and 63 by baseline serostatus. Statistical analyses were descriptive and included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of RSVt. Missing data were not imputed; 95% CI used the Clopper-Pearson method. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04491877); the trial closed to enrolment on April 13, 2023. FINDINGS: Between Sept 10, 2020, and April 13, 2023, 180 participants in cohort 4 were randomly assigned to RSVt-LD (n=61; females, 31 [51%] of 61), RSVt-HD (n=58; females, 25 [43%] of 58), or placebo (n=61; females, 32 [52%] of 61). The mean age at enrolment was 10·4 months (SD 3·1) in the RSVt-LD, 10·6 months (SD 3·6) in the RSVt-HD, and 10·6 months (SD 3·8) in the placebo groups; most participants (>60%) were younger than 12 months in all three groups. The majority of participants (>65%) in all three groups were Hispanic or Latino. Participants were categorised as those with (RSV-experienced) or without (RSV-naive) previous RSV exposure. RSV-naive group was further classified as participants who were RSV-seronegative (no maternal antibody present) and RSV-passive-positive (having passive maternal RSV antibodies). Among the RSV-naive participants, on day 84, after the first or second vaccine administration, four-fold or higher increases in RSV-neutralising antibodies were observed in 19 of 28 (67·9%, 95% CI 47·6-84·1) participants in the RSVt-LD group, 13 of 21 (61·9%, 95% CI 38·4-81·9) participants in the RSVt-HD group, and two of 27 (7·4%, 95% CI 0·9-24·3) participants in the placebo group. Detectable shedding on day 7 occurred in 22 of 41 (53·7%, 95% CI 37·4-69·3) RSV-naive participants in the RSVt-LD group and 17 of 30 (56·7%, 95% CI 37·4-74·5) participants in the RSVt-HD group. Among RSV-naive participants who were RSV-seronegative, on day 84, four-fold or higher rises were observed in 15 of 20 (75·0%, 95% CI 50·9-91·3) participants in the RSVt-LD group, ten of 11 (90·9%, 95% CI 58·7-99·8) participants in the RSVt-HD group, and two of 15 (13·3%, 95% CI 1·7-40·5) participants in the placebo group; shedding on day 7 occurred in 17 of 28 (60·7%, 95% CI 40·6-78·5) participants in the RSVt-LD group and 11 of 18 (61·1%, 35·7-82·7) participants in the RSVt-HD group. Among RSV-naive participants who were RSV-passive-positive, on day 84, four-fold or higher rises were observed in four of eight (50·0%, 95% CI 15·7-84·3) participants in the RSVt-LD group, three of ten (30·0%, 95% CI 6·7-65·2) participants in the RSVt-HD group, and 0 of 12 (0, 95% CI 0·0-26·5) participants in the placebo group; shedding on day 7 occurred in five of 13 (38·5%, 95% CI 13·9-68·4) participants in the RSVt-LD group and six of 12 (50·0%, 95% CI 21·1-78·9) participants in the RSVt-HD group. Among RSV-experienced participants, on day 84, four-fold or higher rises were observed in two of 14 (14·3%, 95% CI 1·8-42·8) participants in the RSVt-LD group, one of 20 (5·0%, 95% CI 0·1-24·9) participants in the RSVt-HD group, and three of 23 (13·0%, 95% CI 2·8-33·6) participants in the placebo group; shedding on day 7 occurred in three of 14 (21·4%, 95% CI 4·7-50·8) RSV-experienced participants in the RSVt-LD group and three of 22 (13·6%, 95% CI 2·9-34·9) participants in the RSVt-HD group. No quantifiable shedding was observed in placebo recipients. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were reported. INTERPRETATION: RSVt induced immune responses and vaccine virus shedding, indicating viral replication and immune priming. RSVt induced greater neutralising antibody responses in RSV-naive participants than in RSV-experienced participants, indicating that baseline serostatus influences vaccine immunogenicity. The discordance between serum antibody responses and viral shedding suggests that serum measures alone might not fully capture vaccine-induced immunity. These findings support further evaluation of live-attenuated intranasal RSV vaccines and highlight the importance of baseline serostatus in interpreting immunogenicity outcomes. FUNDING: Sanofi.

title: Airborne transmission risk of monkeypox virus: the importance of infection-competent virus
abstract: Zhaoliang Chen and colleagues1 propose that quantitative PCR (qPCR) cycle threshold (Ct) values exceeding 35 in massive-volume air sampling should not be equated with airborne transmissibility for monkeypox virus. Although this opinion might have practical utility, it does not address the fundamental biological basis for estimating transmissibility: the material being detected must be infectious for there to be transmission potential. We argue that a Ct value alone should not be considered as evidence of transmission potential, as qPCR cannot distinguish between nucleic acid from infection-competent virions and nucleic acid from degraded virions that pose no infection potential and therefore no transmission potential.

title: Implementation of rapid pan-microbial metagenomics in paediatric intensive care: a single-centre, prospective, observational study
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical metagenomics studies have rarely reported rapid results with clinical impact, or deployment of protocols to centres beyond where they were developed. We describe the implementation of a previously validated rapid pan-microbial respiratory metagenomics service to paediatric intensive care, reporting modifications, feasibility, performance, clinical impact, and staff views. Methods Single-centre prospective interventional study of a metagenomics service testing respiratory samples from paediatric ICU patients at a London hospital between November 2024 and February 2025. This was based on a well-established published workflow detecting bacteria, fungi, and DNA/RNA viruses, with same-day preliminary results and next-day final results. Performance was assessed against routine microbiology. Clinical impact (change in antimicrobials, diagnosis or infection control) was evaluated through electronic health record review. Clinical staff were surveyed via an anonymous online semi-structured questionnaire. Findings 177 samples from 122 patients were tested. 174/177 (98%) passed quality control. Sensitivity at 16 hours sequencing was 89% (95% CI 80-95) for bacteria, 100% (95% CI 54-100) for fungi, and 87% (95% CI 76-95) for viruses, with specificities ≥99% across all kingdoms. Metagenomics identified 50 additional pathogens in 42/174 (24%) samples, all confirmed by orthogonal PCR testing. Clinical impact occurred in 51/174 (29.3%) samples, consisting of antimicrobial changes in 46/174 (26.4%), including 16/174 (9.2%) cessations and 10/174 (5.7%) initiations, and four samples (2.3%) with infection control implications. Among ICU staff surveyed (n=33), 72% viewed metagenomics positively, 0% viewing it negatively, and 67% perceived additional benefit over routine testing. Interpretation This clinical pilot of rapid respiratory metagenomics in paediatric intensive care demonstrated high specificity and good sensitivity. Protocols developed for an adult population were adapted to a paediatric population, including for polymicrobial upper respiratory tract samples that are more common for children. However, increased sensitivity and AMR prediction will be required to be truly disruptive. Whilst changes in patient management were observed, particularly for antimicrobial stewardship, delineating the true contribution of mNGS results is difficult in this study. Multi-centre studies over multiple winter seasons, with control arms and rationalising of patient cohorts and samples, are needed to assess impact on patient outcomes and cost-effectiveness. Research in Context Evidence before this study Metagenomic next generation sequencing (mNGS) is increasingly being used in clinical settings for the diagnosis of infection. Technical performance of mNGS versus routine testing is frequently reported, but few studies report clinical impact of mNGS. Even rarer are studies reporting the adaptation of an established protocol from the centre of its development to a new centre with a different patient population (paediatric). We searched PubMed for studies published between 1st Jan 2020 and 1st Jan 2025, using the terms “paediatrics” AND “metagenomics” AND “treatment” AND either “respiratory” OR “pneumonia”. This search returned 135 abstracts, of which three were prospective studies using respiratory metagenomic testing in a fashion which impacted patient care. Of these, one study was not configured to detect RNA viruses. The remaining two studies reported 318 paediatric cases undergoing metagenomics. Neither study reported same day reporting of results with the intention of providing actionable results in real time. In summary there is minimal literature on the use of metagenomics as a rapid diagnostic test for respiratory infections in paediatric intensive care, or of adapting adult metagenomic protocols to paediatric populations. Added value of this study This observational prospective study is the first to show adaptation of a same day mNGS protocol able to detect bacteria, fungi, DNA and RNA viruses in a paediatric population. We show that modification of the adult protocol to include more upper respiratory and polymicrobial specimens was successful in achieving comparable performance standards. Metagenomics more rapidly identified bacterial pathogens which were also detected by standard-of-care methods as well as additional organisms that were not identified by routine methods. Taken together the data shows impact on antimicrobial prescribing, which could have implications for antimicrobial stewardship and clinical outcomes, although currently the precise contribution of mNGS to these antimicrobial prescribing decisions is unclear. Implications of all the available evidence This data suggests a role for respiratory metagenomics for diagnosing respiratory infection in paediatric intensive care. The results show the feasibility of implementing adult protocols in paediatric populations. Randomised control trials and cost-benefit analyses are still needed to assess true impact on length of hospital stay, clinical outcomes, antimicrobial usage and mortality.

title: Bourbon virus: an expanding tick-borne threat hidden by diagnostic blind spots
abstract: Tick-borne viruses have emerged as a growing public health concern, causing clinical symptoms that range from mild febrile illness to severe encephalitis and haemorrhagic fever. In the USA, two emerging human-infecting tick-borne viruses were identified: Heartland virus (formerly Bandavirus heartlandense) in 2009 and Bourbon virus (formerly Thogotovirus bourbonense) in 2014. Bourbon virus was initially considered a rare tick-borne virus geographically restricted to the midwestern USA. However, the virus appears to have expanded into the more densely populated southeastern and northeastern regions, as evidenced by an increasing number of reported Bourbon virus-positive cases among patients with tick exposure.

title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs. METHODS: In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. FINDINGS: Among 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%. INTERPRETATION: No single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice. FUNDING: UK National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Research Charitable Trust Fund of the Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.

title: Antibiotic overuse and mortality in patients hospitalised for COVID-19: a global cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Global antibiotic use during the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact remain unclear. This study analysed antibiotic use, bacterial co-infections, and the association between antibiotic use and in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalised for COVID-19, using a WHO database. METHODS: We conducted a multicountry cohort study using anonymised patient-level data from The WHO Global Clinical Platform for COVID-19. Data were collected across 64 countries in all six WHO regions between January, 2020, and October, 2023. The study included hospitalised patients of all ages with suspected or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. We obtained patient-level data from standardised WHO case report forms completed prospectively or retrospectively and from harmonised national registries, research studies, and hospital databases. Patients without a suspected or confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or missing information on hospital admission date, antibiotic use, or outcome were excluded from the analysis. Patients were followed up from hospital admission until death, discharge, transfer, or 28 days, whichever occurred first. Follow-up data were collected at hospital discharge or death by the treating facility and entered into the platform. The primary outcome was 28-day in-hospital mortality, and we analysed this outcome using Cox proportional hazards models with a shared frailty term to account for country-level clustering. FINDINGS: The median age of the study population was 61·9 years (±21·7), with 198 223 women and 251 990 men with data available on antibiotic use. Of the 592 898 patients enrolled, 451 291 (76·1%) had data on antibiotic use and were included in the descriptive analysis; 122 854 had complete data on empirical treatment type, of whom 47 359 (38·5%) were included in the regression analysis. Among the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use, 341 125 (75·6%) received antibiotics, more frequently in severe to critical cases than in mild to moderate cases (80·5% vs 71·6%). Prescribing was highest in the Eastern Mediterranean (83·0%) and African (82·7%) regions and lowest in the Western Pacific region (32·8%), declining in the European region and region of the Americas but increasing in the African region between 2020 and 2022. Treatment was predominantly empirical and involved Watch antibiotics of the WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve classification. Clinically suspected co-infections were reported in 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 patients; among those with positive cultures, 1815 (42·8%) of 4237 had multidrug-resistant bacteria. In the unadjusted analyses, empirical antibiotic use was associated with higher mortality across severity strata. After adjustment for age, sex, comorbidities, and disease severity, empirical antibiotic use remained associated with increased mortality in mild to moderate cases (adjusted hazard ratio 1·80, 95% CI 1·36-2·38) and severe to critical cases (1·16, 1·08-1·24). INTERPRETATION: Despite clinically suspected co-infections being reported in only 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 enrolled patients, 341 125 (75·6%) of the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use received antibiotic therapy, predominantly broad-spectrum agents. As antibiotic use was not associated with improved clinical outcomes and is known to increase antimicrobial resistance, it should be rationalised through strengthened antimicrobial stewardship and behavioural interventions, particularly during respiratory viral epidemics. FUNDING: None.

title: Phylogeographical structure and genetic introgression in Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli: a genomic epidemiology study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli (S Napoli), a non-typhoidal Salmonella serotype that has been emerging in Italy, Switzerland, and France since the mid-1990s, has an unusual epidemiological profile that suggests a role for the environment in the transmission of these bacteria. The genomics of S Napoli has been inadequately characterised; we, therefore, aimed to provide a robust genomic framework for S Napoli surveillance. METHODS: In this genomic epidemiology study, we performed short-read sequencing of 1145 S Napoli isolates from national surveillance in four European countries (Italy, Switzerland, France, and Spain) and complemented this dataset with 175 additional genomes (174 published and one unpublished). We used the EnteroBase core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme and its associated Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, along with other genome-based bioinformatics approaches such as single nucleotide variant-based phylogenetic analyses, ResFinder, PlasmidFinder, and RefSeq genomes, to characterise population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence, and differences in gene content among genetic lineages. FINDINGS: We analysed 1320 S Napoli genomes, collected between April, 1945, and September 14, 2022, from human (n=1088, 82·4%) and non-human (n=232, 17·6%) sources in Italy (n=317, 24%), Switzerland (n=181, 13·7%), France (n=773, 58·5%), and Spain (n=48, 3·6%), confirming that the rising prevalence of S Napoli is driven by a single monophyletic serotype within cgMLST superlineage HC2000_1289. However, this serotype displays considerable genetic diversity (15 lineages falling into 12 HC900 clusters), strong spatial structuring, and a low frequency (2%) of AMR determinants. We also detected genetic introgression between S Napoli and the sympatric, closely related Salmonella enterica serotype Veneziana. INTERPRETATION: Unlike successful non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes, for which globalisation has had a homogenising effect, S Napoli forms distinct lineages isolated by geographical distance. This study suggests that the persistence of S Napoli as a geographically structured metapopulation, causing localised human infections, could reflect the natural ecology of Salmonella before the rise of agribusiness. Future research should investigate the environmental reservoirs and transmission pathways of S Napoli. FUNDING: Fondation Le Roch-Les Mousquetaires, Institut Pasteur, Santé publique France, Investissement d'Avenir programme, Laboratoire d'Excellence 'Integrative Biology of Emerging Infectious Diseases', and Institute of Health Carlos III 'Acción Estratégica de Salud Intramural'.

title: Cholera rapid diagnostic test performance at the host–microbe interface: a prospective longitudinal study in Bangladesh
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Effective cholera outbreak response requires accurate bedside rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) because access to laboratories is often limited. Formative studies suggest cholera diagnostics have multiple vulnerabilities, including antibiotics and predation by bacteriophage (‘phage’) specific to Vibrio cholerae ( Vc ). Methods We conducted a prospective nationwide study in Bangladesh among over 2000 patients with diarrhoeal disease to characterize how these vulnerabilities impact RDT performance. Assays included culture, qPCR and mass spectrometry. Findings With the current gold standard of culture or qPCR Vc positivity, we found no effect of phage on RDT performance. When the diagnostic criteria were expanded to include phage, there was a small decrease in RDT sensitivity. In contrast, large increases in sensitivity and specificity were observed among patients with moderate and severe dehydration. Using the expanded definition, the odds of RDT positivity decreased among cholera patients with phage exposure. The effect was most robust among patients with severe dehydration. Antibiotic were detected in over 80% of samples by LC-MS/MS which limited testing for effects on RDTs. Applying these findings, we estimated that restricting RDT use to severe patients with no reported antibiotic exposure increases sensitivity by 50% compared to unrestricted use. If phage were a diagnostic proxy for Vc , we estimate RDT would miss an additional 17% of cholera cases. Interpretation Cholera RDTs have critical limitations that require consideration in global deployments. Inclusion of phage detection in diagnostic criteria may improve case detection which requires further study. The impact of these findings likely extends to other diseases where diagnostics share similar vulnerabilities. RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Evidence before this study We conducted two Pubmed searches for reports published after Jan 1, 2000, in all languages. The first search terms were [bacteriophage OR phage] AND [pathogen] AND [diagnostic test]. The primary search criteria identified 57 publications. A secondary criterion excluded reviews and papers on phage display technology. Among twenty remaining articles, bacteriophage were used as proxies for pathogens within diverse genera (Yersinia, Mycobacterium, Burkholderia, Staphylococcus, Salmonella, Bacillus, Escherichia, Acinetobacter, Vibrio); phage profiles were also used as biomarkers for infection. The second search terms were [rapid diagnostic test OR RDT] AND [Vibrio]. After excluding reviews, 101 papers were identified that covered immunologic (antibody-based lateral flow assays), molecular (PCR, qPCR, nl-qPCR) and mass spectrometry-based assays; only 5 articles related to vibriophage detection of which three were permutations of the same initiative. Added value of this study To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the vulnerabilities of RDT performance (e.g., sensitivity and specificity) to virulent bacteriophage and antibiotics in a large multi-site study. The hypothesis that antimicrobials and disease severity might impact RDT performance by decreasing or increasing the target number, respectively, is not novel. However, there is a lack of literature from large clinical studies that rigorously tests this hypothesis. Therefore, the added value of this study is a pragmatic evaluation of this hypothesis and a proof of concept for how to test these complex questions for other less tractable diseases. Implications of all the available evidence Inside the cholera field, we applied the findings by estimating that changing to a mode of restricted RDT use in which RDTs are reserved for severely dehydrated patients who report no antibiotic exposure, significantly improves the sensitivity. Furthermore, we estimate that an additional 17% of cases would be missed by RDT if the case definition were expanded to include phage detection as a proxy for the pathogen. In this context, the RDT remains with limitations that require consideration when optimizing global RDT deployments. Implications likely extend to other diseases where diagnostics share similar vulnerabilities.

title: Antimicrobial selection is only part of the story: from resistance to persistence
abstract: As global projections warn of escalating mortality from bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) through 2050,1 understanding how antimicrobial prescribing shapes multidrug resistance is a clinical priority.2,3 In The Lancet Microbe, Thi Mui Pham and colleagues provide a 15-year perspective on this problem through a retrospective cohort analysis of 84 657 hospital-onset isolates, encompassing Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, from 138 US Veterans Affairs medical centres.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex strain discordance among people with tuberculosis and a history of household contact: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Tuberculosis disease clusters within households, but the proportion of disease among household contacts that results from recent within-household transmission remains unclear. We aimed to estimate the prevalence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex strain discordance among pairs of individuals with tuberculosis and a history of household contact, and the proportion of all tuberculosis disease attributable to recent household transmission. Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we included empirical studies or systematic reviews published in English from Jan 1, 1985, to Jan 26, 2024, that described at least ten pairs of individuals with a history of household contact, in which both people had active tuberculosis and their isolates were strain-typed using RFLP, mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit–variable-number tandem repeat, or whole-genome sequencing. We excluded studies that only collected data on residence for isolates of the same strain and studies that used preselection for both index and secondary cases. Searches of MEDLINE, Embase, Global Health, Web of Science, and POPLINE databases were updated on Jan 26, 2024. Titles and abstracts and then full texts were screened, and data were extracted independently, by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Summary data were extracted from published reports; when necessary, we contacted study authors, some of whom reanalysed data. The main outcome was the prevalence of strain discordance among pairs of individuals with tuberculosis and a history of household contact. Our main analyses excluded studies using 12-loci or 15-loci mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit–variable-number tandem repeat and studies performed during tuberculosis outbreaks, as these were considered to be at high risk of bias. We used an inverse variance heterogeneity model applying a double-arcsine transformation to stabilise variance. The proportion of total variability due to between-study heterogeneity was estimated using I 2 . We estimated the proportion of all tuberculosis attributable to recent household transmission as the product of strain concordance and the proportion of all cases in the community with a history of household exposure to a putative index case, which we derived from external data. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to the choice of model and to varying assumptions about household size when estimating the attributable fraction. Our PROSPERO registration number was CRD42024504096. Findings The updated searches identified an additional 3735 unique records. Thirty studies from 18 countries met the inclusion criteria. Four studies were omitted from the meta-analysis because they were at high risk of bias. The remaining 26 studies comprised 1544 index–secondary patient pairs. A high proportion of total variability was due to between-study heterogeneity (I 2 90·3, 95% CI 69·0–95·3%). The overall pooled estimate of the prevalence of strain discordance was 0·47 (95% CI 0·32–0·62). Pooled estimates differed by tuberculosis incidence: 0·30 (0·25–0·34) in low-incidence settings, 0·25 (0·15–0·36) in moderate-incidence settings, and 0·59 (0·41–0·76) in high-incidence settings (p=0·003). The median proportion of tuberculosis disease attributable to recent household transmission was 10·8% (range 1·4–21·1%). Interpretation Strain discordance is common, particularly in high-incidence settings. These findings suggest that recent household transmission makes a small contribution to the overall burden of tuberculosis disease. In this study, the number of household pairs and geographical diversity of the studies were strengths. Between-study heterogeneity limited precision. Our estimates of attributable fraction relied on external data. Strain discordance does not necessarily imply discordance in drug susceptibility. These results should motivate a greater focus on social protection and interrupting community transmission. Funding None.

title: US CDC’s 5-day recommendation of the artemether–lumefantrine regimen: lessons from Africa and travellers
abstract: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has extended treatment recommendation for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria with artemether–lumefantrine (AL) regimen from 3 days and six doses to 5 days and ten doses. This decision is striking not because AL has become ineffective, but because it exposes a widening gap between molecular markers of resistance and clinical treatment failure.1

title: Expanding Epstein–Barr virus-associated disease burden prioritises vaccine development
abstract: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) establishes lifelong infection in more than 90% of adults. Long recognised as the cause of infectious mononucleosis and several malignancies, EBV is increasingly linked to autoimmune and other immune-mediated diseases (appendix p 1). Seroconversion was associated with a 32-fold increase in multiple sclerosis risk, whereas further evidence links EBV to systemic lupus erythematosus and other immune-mediated disorders.1,2

title: Diversity analysis of indoor and outdoor fungal bioaerosols: methodological considerations
abstract: We read with interest the Article by Samuel J Hemmings and colleagues,1 published in The Lancet Microbe, which reports that indoor airborne fungal communities in urban UK homes are more diverse than outdoor communities. Quantifying indoor airborne fungal DNA might help to identify epidemiologically informed exposure thresholds to guide policy making; however, potential methodological biases warrant attention.

title: Novel dengue serotype 4 live virus human challenge: a phase 1 dose optimisation and homologous rechallenge study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Dengue live virus human challenges (LVHCs) are key in dengue vaccine and pharmacological development, to down-select candidates and provide a useful platform for understanding viral-host immunology in a controlled setting. The primary aim of this study was to assess the safety, reactogenicity, and immunogenicity of a newly derived underattenuated dengue virus serotype-4-LVHC (DENV-4-LVHC) strain intended for future dengue challenge studies. METHODS: We conducted a first-in-human, phase 1, non-randomised, open-label study that evaluated the safety and optimised dose of the DENV-4-LVHC strain H-241 in flavivirus-naive healthy adult volunteers. The trial was conducted between April 28, 2022, and Dec 18, 2023, at the University of Maryland (Baltimore, MD, USA) and included a dose-optimisation study in which participants were enrolled into staggered-start, dose-ranging cohorts, beginning with the lowest dose, and homologous rechallenge substudy in which willing, primary-infected participants were rechallenged with the optimised dose of DENV-4 at least 12 months from the primary challenge. Successful challenge was defined as more than 90% participants developing self-limiting mild-to-moderate dengue symptoms with detectable RNAemia. Participants were analysed on the basis of the treatment group (primary infection vs rechallenge). This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05268302). FINDINGS: 14 healthy adult participants were enrolled between March 31, 2022, and June 9, 2022 (dose optimisation), and were challenged with a subcutaneous dose of DENV-4-LVHC on June 12, 2023 (rechallenge). The majority were men (11 [79%] of 14), and almost half were non-White (6 [43%]). The mean participant age was 33·6 years (range 20-48). All 14 participants developed viraemia and symptoms consistent with self-limited, mild-to-moderate dengue at an optimised dose of 95 plaque-forming units (low dose). Six (60%) participants (of the original ten from the 2022 cohort) were rechallenged using the optimised dose 1 year after primary challenge, and none developed detectable dengue. Robust antibody responses, plasmablast expansion, and antiviral gene upregulation were seen during primary infection but not after rechallenge. No severe dengue, need for inpatient observation, or dengue challenge-related serious adverse events were observed. INTERPRETATION: DENV-4-LVHC was found to be safe and highly predictable for use in future challenge studies, to evaluate vaccine and therapeutic candidates. Immunity from previous DENV-4-LVHC infection conferred protection following homologous rechallenge 1 year after primary exposure. FUNDING: Military Infectious Disease Research Program; Medical Technology Enterprise Consortium.

title: Clinical and immunological correlates of CXCR4 coreceptor use in people with HIV-1 receiving antiretroviral therapy in the Netherlands: a multicentre cohort study
abstract: Background CXCR4-using (X4) viruses are associated with faster disease progression in untreated HIV-1 infection, although their clinical, virological, and immunological correlates during suppressive antiretroviral therapy are not well characterised. We aimed to assess the associations between X4 coreceptor use and clinical outcomes, HIV persistence, and immunological profiles in people with HIV-1 receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy. Methods In this multicentre cohort study, asymptomatic adults with HIV receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy were enrolled from four HIV treatment centres in the Netherlands between Oct 16, 2019, and Oct 27, 2021 and followed up for 2 years. Clinical data were obtained from structured questionnaires and electronic health records. HIV-1 coreceptor use was predicted from triplicate env sequencing with Geno2pheno, and participants were classified as having CCR5-using (R5), X4, or mixed virus. HIV-1 subtype was assigned using env and pol sequences. Total and intact HIV DNA in CD4 + T cells were quantified using multiplex digital PCR. Plasma proteomics, bulk peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics, and high-dimensional flow cytometry were used for systems-level profiling. Associations between predicted coreceptor use and clinical outcomes, HIV-reservoir measures, and immunological profiles were assessed using adjusted regression models and discovery and validation cohorts. Findings Coreceptor use was assigned in 1724 participants; 1222 had R5 virus, 336 had X4 virus, and 166 had mixed classifications. Primary clinical analyses included 1494 participants, of whom 1172 were in the R5 group and 322 were in the X4 group. Compared with the R5 group, the X4 group had a lower CD4 + nadir, a higher prevalence of previous AIDS-defining events, poorer immunological recovery, and more comorbidities, particularly type 2 diabetes and non-affective psychiatric disorders. The median total HIV DNA was 1051 copies per 10 6 CD4 + T cells in the X4 group versus 599 copies per 10 6 CD4 + T cells in the R5 group, and the median intact HIV DNA was 23 copies per 10 6 CD4 + T cells versus 15 copies per 10 6 CD4 + T cells. No significant differences were observed in plasma inflammatory proteins. Participants in the X4 group had higher frequencies of activated CD4 + T cells and PD-1 + regulatory T cells, and transcriptomic analyses identified downregulation of two validated transcripts involved in transcriptional repression and lipid hydrolysis. Interpretation Among people with HIV receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy, infection with X4 virus was associated with markers of more advanced previous HIV disease, impaired immune recovery, larger HIV reservoirs, and selected comorbidities despite viral suppression. Coreceptor use might therefore help to contextualise clinical, virological, and immunological heterogeneity in treated HIV-1 infection and could be relevant to future HIV cure studies. Funding ViiV Healthcare.

title: Nigeria responds to Ebola Bundibugyo virus case
abstract: Nigeria is tracing contacts and strengthening infection prevention measures after confirming an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital city, as the ongoing outbreak tests the country’s ability to detect infections and prevent transmission within health-care facilities.

title: Africa needs to help model the future of tuberculosis vaccines
abstract: The tuberculosis (TB) vaccine pipeline is entering a new era. As da Costa and colleagues noted in their Series, 18 vaccine candidates are in clinical development, including six in phase 3.1,2 M72/AS01E has shown approximately 50% activity against pulmonary TB disease in infected adults, with phase 3 evaluation under way.1,2 These advances offer an unprecedented opportunity to accelerate progress towards End TB targets. However, they also raise a neglected question: who will generate the modelling evidence that determines where, when, and how these vaccines should be used?

title: Intracellular Staphylococcus aureus in human infections: evidence from clinical specimens
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen causing extensive morbidity and mortality. In vitro and animal studies show that S aureus can invade and survive within host cells. Such intracellular reservoirs might impair antibiotic and immune clearance, yet their clinical relevance in humans remains controversial. Here, we review 33 human studies published between 1984 and 2025 that assess the occurrence of intracellular S aureus across diverse disease conditions. We critically evaluated the methods used to detect intracellular S aureus in human biopsies and evidence across different tissues and diseases. Although the strength of evidence varies across studies, the overall findings strongly suggest the presence of S aureus within diverse human cell types. These findings could have important implications for diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. We identify key knowledge gaps, including the relative proportions of intracellular and extracellular S aureus, viability of intracellular bacteria, and persistence of these bacteria during antibiotic exposure. Thus, our analysis highlights intracellular states as a relevant part of S aureus biology in human infections and identifies future research directions.

title: Could the next pandemic be fungal and could we respond effectively? From plausible pathways to operational preparedness
abstract: Fungal diseases cause substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet they have been persistently neglected in pandemic preparedness plans, largely because no sustained human-to-human fungal pandemic has been documented to date. However, multidisciplinary evidence challenges the assumption that fungi are irrelevant to pandemic risk. Wildlife fungal pandemics show that mycoses can emerge on a global scale with catastrophic and irreversible consequences. Moreover, climate change is narrowing the mammalian thermal barrier against fungi, favouring heat-tolerant species, reshaping their global distribution, and thus facilitating zoonotic spillover. Rising human susceptibility-driven by ageing populations, immunomodulatory therapies, and increasingly complex health care-is intersecting with a substantial therapeutic gap, characterised by the absence of licensed vaccines, a limited range of antifungal agents, and increasing antimicrobial resistance. In this Personal View, we move beyond a synthesis of evidence to propose an operational framework for fungal pandemic preparedness, outlining plausible routes to pandemic-scale impact and the surveillance, diagnostic, therapeutic, One Health, and outbreak-response capacities needed to detect and contain emerging fungal threats before they become unmanageable.
